screens.title: Access Control and Authorization in Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: In permissioned Fabric networks, membership alone doesn't mean permission for every action. In this lesson you will learn how to enforce precise, business-level authorization rules inside your chaincode so that only the right person or role can change specific data. We'll focus on retrieving verified identity facts from the transaction context using GetClientIdentity, and on making decisions from MSP IDs or embedded certificate attributes. You will also see how to use transient data to pass sensitive one-time evidence, like a one-time password or external proof, without writing it to the ledger. A concrete example is an asset transfer that only the recorded owner can perform; the chaincode reads the submitter's MSP ID and rejects transfers from other organizations. Common pitfalls include trusting client-supplied owner fields and applying overly permissive org-level checks. By the end you will understand practical patterns—MSP-based ownership checks, attribute-based role checks, and transient-data proofs—that protect sensitive state while keeping authorization auditable and explicit. Which of these patterns will map best to your application's trust model?

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Explore Key Topics

ABAC

Why this matters

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide our practical work in this chapter. First, you will understand why chaincode must implement fine-grained access control beyond network membership, and be able to explain how such controls reduce risk in multi-organization scenarios. Second, you will learn how to retrieve verified identity facts from the transaction context, including MSP identifiers and certificate attributes, and use them in authorization checks. Third, you will implement authorization logic that enforces ownership and role-based constraints, for example preventing non-owners from transferring assets or requiring role:admin to delete documents. Fourth, you will explore transient data as a private channel to pass sensitive authorization proofs without persisting them on the ledger. Each objective pairs a practical task with a reasoning check so you'll not only implement code but also test adversarial cases. For example, when you check GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID(), you'll also test a mismatched MSP to ensure the chaincode rejects the action. These learning goals prepare you to write auditable, least-privilege chaincode that defends data at the application level.

screens.title: How you'll apply these skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives translate to specific practices you will apply immediately. You will modify chaincode functions to derive the caller identity from the transaction context rather than trusting user-supplied fields. For testing, you will simulate calls from different MSPs and from certificates with and without expected attributes to verify behavior. You will implement error handling that returns clear authorization failures so client apps can react. In a hands-on exercise you'll implement CreateDocument and DeleteDocument functions: CreateDocument will only accept calls from Org1MSP, while DeleteDocument will require role:admin in the caller's certificate. You should test both successful and failing cases and review ledger state after failed attempts to confirm nothing sensitive was written. These habits—derive identity from the stub, validate attributes, protect sensitive inputs via transient, and write clear errors—are what make chaincode auditable, maintainable, and resistant to client-side forgery.

screens.title: Why chaincode must implement fine-grained authorization
screens.narratorSegment: In Fabric, network-level policies and MSPs control who may participate, but they don't encode every business rule your application needs. Fine-grained authorization inside chaincode means explicitly checking whether the submitter is allowed to perform a requested action on a particular object. For example, a ledger may store an asset with an owner field representing the owner's MSP. Without checks inside chaincode, any member could attempt to transfer that asset by passing a crafted owner value. The secure pattern is to derive the caller identity from the transaction context and compare it to the stored owner before making state changes. A typical control asserts that ctx. GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID() equals the asset's ownerMSP value. This prevents client-provided owner strings from being trusted. Another reason to perform these checks in chaincode is audibility: authorization failures are explicit and can be surfaced to client applications with clear error messages explaining why a transaction was rejected. A common misconception is that endorsement or channel policies alone enforce application semantics; they do not. The takeaway is to treat chaincode as the last trust boundary where business rules and least privilege must be enforced.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Fine-grained authorization enforces precise application rules inside chaincode so actions are allowed only when verified identity facts meet policy.

content.html:
Core Concept
Fine-grained authorization

Chaincode enforces who may call which function and who may modify specific data by relying on verifiable identity information from the transaction context.

Concrete example
An asset stores ownerMSP; TransferAsset reads the caller's MSP and rejects the transfer when they differ.
Why it matters
Prevents forged client inputs and ensures business rules are enforced consistently across endorsers.
Common misconception
Believing endorsement or channel policies alone enforce fine-grained application rules. They don't substitute chaincode checks.
Guided check list
  • Derive caller identity with ctx.GetClientIdentity() every time authorization is required.
  • Compare caller MSP or attributes to stored ownership or required role values in world state.
  • Do not accept client-supplied owner IDs as authoritative.
  • Return descriptive errors on authorization failures so clients can handle them correctly.
Key Takeaway

Treat chaincode as the final guard for business rules; trust identity from the stub, not client arguments.

screens.title: ClientIdentity methods you can rely on
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric exposes a ClientIdentity object from the transaction context that gives you verified facts about the submitter. The most commonly used methods are GetMSPID, which returns the submitter's organization's MSP ID; GetID, which returns a unique identifier derived from the certificate; GetX509Certificate, which returns the entire certificate for advanced parsing; and GetAttributeValue, which fetches custom attributes embedded in the X.509 certificate. Use GetMSPID for organization-level checks such as allowing only Org1MSP to create certain objects. Use GetAttributeValue when you need role-level control—an example is rejecting DeleteDocument unless the caller has role:admin. GetX509Certificate is powerful but more complex: parsing the certificate to inspect OU or CN fields is possible but error-prone and may tighten coupling to CA configurations. A practical pattern is to prefer GetAttributeValue when the CA already emits attributes, because it's simpler and less brittle than manual certificate parsing. Remember to handle errors from these calls: identity retrieval can fail and should produce clear authorization errors. Which method you choose depends on the level of granularity and your CA's attribute provisioning. ClientIdentity methods you can rely on means choose getmspid for org checks, getattributevalue for abac role checks, and reserve getx509certificate for advanced parsing when necessary.. In practical terms, getmspid, getid, getx509certificate, getattributevalue — what they provide and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ClientIdentity summary
keyIdea.text: Choose GetMSPID for org checks, GetAttributeValue for ABAC role checks, and reserve GetX509Certificate for advanced parsing when necessary.

content.html:
Definition
ClientIdentity methods
GetMSPID() — returns the caller's MSP ID; ideal for organization-level authorization.
GetID() — unique identifier derived from certificate; useful for per-user ownership checks.
GetX509Certificate() — returns full X.509 certificate; useful for deep parsing but more complex.
GetAttributeValue(attr) — reads embedded attributes for ABAC, like role:admin or OU:auditor.
When to pick each
  • Use GetMSPID for coarse org-level constraints.
  • Use GetAttributeValue for roles and ABAC policies provided by your CA.
  • Reserve GetX509Certificate for special parsing when attributes are not available.
Misconception
Parsing certificate fields for authorization is fragile compared to using CA-provided attributes via GetAttributeValue.

screens.title: Owner-based transfer: code walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a transfer function pattern that enforces ownership by checking the caller's MSP. The chaincode reads the asset from world state, unmarshals it, retrieves ctx. GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID(), and then compares that MSP to the asset's Owner field. If they don't match, the chaincode returns an authorization error. This pattern prevents a client from simply passing a different owner value to circumvent checks. A concrete code example is in Go: the TransferAsset function gets the asset bytes, unmarshals into an Asset struct that includes Owner, calls GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID(), and if callingClientMSPID!= asset. Owner it rejects. After authorization passes, the owner is updated and PutState writes the new asset. A common pitfall is forgetting to check for nil asset or unmarshal errors before authorization, which can reveal unintended behavior. When testing, simulate calls from both the owner MSP and a different MSP to confirm the rejection path. The takeaway: derive the caller's identity from the stub for any ownership-based decision. In practical terms, inspect transferasset that requires the caller msp to match asset owner. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Authorize transfers by comparing ctx.GetClientIdentity().GetMSPID() to the stored owner; never trust client-supplied owner arguments.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
TransferAsset authorization
This snippet shows the key authorization block you should include before state mutation.
// --- Authorization Logic ---
callingClientMSPID, err := ctx.GetClientIdentity().GetMSPID()
if err != nil {
  return fmt.Errorf("failed to get calling client MSP ID: %v", err)
}
if callingClientMSPID != asset.Owner {
  return fmt.Errorf("client from MSP %s is not authorized to transfer asset %s. Current owner is %s", callingClientMSPID, assetID, asset.Owner)
}
// --- End Authorization Logic ---
Test idea
Invoke TransferAsset from an identity with the asset owner MSP and from a different MSP to verify acceptance and rejection paths.
Scenario
Asset A is owner Org1MSP. A client from Org2MSP attempts a transfer. The chaincode rejects because the reported caller MSP doesn't match stored owner.
Common mistake

Accepting an ownerID function argument as authoritative lets clients spoof ownership. Always derive identity from ctx.

screens.title: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) vs MSP checks
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between MSP-based checks and ABAC using certificate attributes depends on the authorization granularity you need. MSP checks answer the question: 'Is the caller from organization X?' They are simple and stable, ideal for organization-level constraints like 'only Org1MSP may create documents'. ABAC answers role- or user-specific questions like 'is the caller an auditor or an admin?' when those roles are embedded as attributes in certificates. Use GetAttributeValue to read attributes such as role:admin and enforce role-based operations like DeleteDocument. A benefit of ABAC is flexibility: roles can be issued by the CA and changed by certificate management without code changes. But ABAC requires CA configuration to include attributes and careful handling of absent attributes. A common misconception is that ABAC is always superior; it can be overkill when your policy is purely org-based and MSP checks are sufficient. In practice a hybrid model often works best: use MSP checks for coarse gates and attributes for sensitive role checks. Always provide clear error messages when attributes are missing so administrators can adjust CA-issued certs. Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) vs MSP checks means use msp checks for org-level rules; use abac via getattributevalue for role-level controls when ca emits attributes.. In practical terms, when to use attributes and when msp-level checks are sufficient. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ABAC vs MSP
keyIdea.text: Use MSP checks for org-level rules; use ABAC via GetAttributeValue for role-level controls when CA emits attributes.

content.html:
Comparison
MSP-based checks
  • Simple org-level control
  • Stable mapping to administrative boundaries
  • Use GetMSPID()
ABAC via attributes
  • Role-level or per-user control
  • Requires CA to embed attributes
  • Use GetAttributeValue()
A hybrid approach is common: gate by MSP for coarse access, then use attributes for sensitive operations, and always handle missing attributes explicitly.
Concrete example
CreateDocument: require Org1MSP. DeleteDocument: require attribute role:admin. QueryDocument: no authorization required.
Pro Tip

If attributes may be absent, fail explicitly with a message that directs admins to the CA configuration needed to include them.

screens.title: Transient data for private authorization proofs
screens.narratorSegment: Transient data is a mechanism to pass confidential values to chaincode that should not be persisted to the world state. The client includes a transient map in the proposal; endorsing peers and chaincode see the data but only a hash is recorded on the ledger. This is ideal for one-time proofs such as a one-time password, external token, or ephemeral signature used to authorize a specific action. In authorization scenarios, the chaincode fetches stub. GetTransient(), consumes the proof to validate the request, and then discards the sensitive value. A concrete use is a transfer that requires a signed external approval token: the token is sent in transient so it is verified by endorsers but never stored. Common mistakes include accidentally putting transient values into state or returning them in responses. Also, transient data is visible to endorsers, so endorsement policy configuration still matters. The simple rule: keep short-lived secrets in transient, validate them in chaincode, and never persist them. When you design tests, assert that only the hash appears on the ledger after the transaction completes. Transient data for private authorization proofs means use stub.gettransient() for ephemeral authorization proofs so secret values are not written to the ledger.. In practical terms, pass sensitive one-time data without writing it to the ledger. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transient summary
keyIdea.text: Use stub.GetTransient() for ephemeral authorization proofs so secret values are not written to the ledger.

content.html:
Definition
Transient data

A proposal-level map for confidential, ephemeral values visible to endorsers and chaincode but not persisted on the ledger. Only a hash is stored.

Concrete usage
Client sends an approval token inside transient; chaincode validates the token and proceeds. The token itself is not PutState'd so it never appears on ledger.
Safety note
Do not write transient values into world state or logs. Only their hash should be visible on ledger records.
Try this

In tests, include transient data when invoking and confirm the ledger contains no sensitive value, only a hash if recorded by your application logic.

keyIdea.text: Combine MSP checks for organization-level control and GetAttributeValue for role checks; test both success and failure cases.

content.html:
Code Template (excerpt)
clientMSPID, err := ctx.GetClientIdentity().GetMSPID()
if err != nil {
  return fmt.Errorf("failed to get client MSP ID: %v", err)
}
if clientMSPID != "Org1MSP" {

screens.title: Error handling and auditability
screens.narratorSegment: Good authorization is not only about denying the wrong actor; it's also about clear error handling and auditability. When authorization fails, return a specific error that explains the reason, such as 'caller MSP X is not authorized to transfer asset Y' or 'attribute role not present'. These messages help client applications provide actionable feedback and help operators diagnose CA or certificate configuration issues. From an audit perspective, chaincode should avoid logging secrets while ensuring that authorization failures are visible in transaction responses and peer logs. Also test failure paths explicitly: attempt restricted calls from unauthorized identities and confirm that the ledger state has not changed and that the error reason is clear. Another key practice is to validate presence of required data—such as confirming GetAttributeValue found the attribute—before assuming it exists. A common mistake is to return generic errors like 'permission denied' without context; that wastes time in triage. Design your error messages to be helpful, non-sensitive, and consistent so both developers and operators can quickly respond. Error handling and auditability means return explicit, non-sensitive errors on authorization failures and validate absence of side effects to keep the ledger auditable.. In practical terms, return meaningful authorization errors and test rejection paths. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Trust boundary: what to trust and what to derive
screens.narratorSegment: A central security principle in chaincode is the trust boundary: chaincode must not trust data provided by the client for authorization decisions. Client arguments can be forged. Instead, derive identity from verified sources supplied by Fabric: the ClientIdentity methods accessible through ctx. GetClientIdentity() and transient data from the proposal. For ownership checks, compare ctx. GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID() or GetID() to the stored owner. For roles, use GetAttributeValue and explicitly handle the attribute not found case. Another aspect of the trust boundary is endorsements: chaincode authorization logic is enforced by endorsers, so ensure your endorsement policy matches the trust model for who should validate those checks. A common error is to rely only on client-side checks or UI gating; always enforce in chaincode to prevent replay or forged requests. Finally, when you use transient data for proofs, remember endorsers will see it—so combine with appropriate endorsement policies to limit exposure where necessary. The chaincode is the final authority for business rules; make sure it derives, validates, and logs authorization decisions responsibly. screens.title: Testing and deployment checklist for authorization
screens.narratorSegment: Thorough testing is essential to ensure your authorization logic behaves as intended when deployed. Start by creating test identities for each MSP and for users with different attributes. Use your test network to invoke CreateDocument and TransferAsset from those identities and assert expected responses. For negative tests, ensure rejected transactions do not modify world state. When testing ABAC, verify that the CA issues the required attributes in the certificate and that GetAttributeValue returns both a value and a found flag. Also test transient workflows by including ephemeral proofs in invocations and confirming those secrets are not present in world state or peer logs. fullNarratorScript:
In permissioned Fabric networks, membership alone doesn't mean permission for every action. In this lesson you will learn how to enforce precise, business-level authorization rules inside your chaincode so that only the right person or role can change specific data. We'll focus on retrieving verified identity facts from the transaction context using GetClientIdentity, and on making decisions from MSP IDs or embedded certificate attributes. You will also see how to use transient data to pass sensitive one-time evidence, like a one-time password or external proof, without writing it to the ledger. A concrete example is an asset transfer that only the recorded owner can perform; the chaincode reads the submitter's MSP ID and rejects transfers from other organizations. Common pitfalls include trusting client-supplied owner fields and applying overly permissive org-level checks. By the end you will understand practical patterns—MSP-based ownership checks, attribute-based role checks, and transient-data proofs—that protect sensitive state while keeping authorization auditable and explicit. Which of these patterns will map best to your application's trust model?

These objectives guide our practical work in this chapter. First, you will understand why chaincode must implement fine-grained access control beyond network membership, and be able to explain how such controls reduce risk in multi-organization scenarios. Second, you will learn how to retrieve verified identity facts from the transaction context, including MSP identifiers and certificate attributes, and use them in authorization checks. Third, you will implement authorization logic that enforces ownership and role-based constraints, for example preventing non-owners from transferring assets or requiring role:admin to delete documents. Fourth, you will explore transient data as a private channel to pass sensitive authorization proofs without persisting them on the ledger. Each objective pairs a practical task with a reasoning check so you'll not only implement code but also test adversarial cases. For example, when you check GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID(), you'll also test a mismatched MSP to ensure the chaincode rejects the action. These learning goals prepare you to write auditable, least-privilege chaincode that defends data at the application level.

These objectives translate to specific practices you will apply immediately. You will modify chaincode functions to derive the caller identity from the transaction context rather than trusting user-supplied fields. For testing, you will simulate calls from different MSPs and from certificates with and without expected attributes to verify behavior. You will implement error handling that returns clear authorization failures so client apps can react. In a hands-on exercise you'll implement CreateDocument and DeleteDocument functions: CreateDocument will only accept calls from Org1MSP, while DeleteDocument will require role:admin in the caller's certificate. You should test both successful and failing cases and review ledger state after failed attempts to confirm nothing sensitive was written. These habits—derive identity from the stub, validate attributes, protect sensitive inputs via transient, and write clear errors—are what make chaincode auditable, maintainable, and resistant to client-side forgery.

In Fabric, network-level policies and MSPs control who may participate, but they don't encode every business rule your application needs. Fine-grained authorization inside chaincode means explicitly checking whether the submitter is allowed to perform a requested action on a particular object. For example, a ledger may store an asset with an owner field representing the owner's MSP. Without checks inside chaincode, any member could attempt to transfer that asset by passing a crafted owner value. The secure pattern is to derive the caller identity from the transaction context and compare it to the stored owner before making state changes. A typical control asserts that ctx. GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID() equals the asset's ownerMSP value. This prevents client-provided owner strings from being trusted. Another reason to perform these checks in chaincode is audibility: authorization failures are explicit and can be surfaced to client applications with clear error messages explaining why a transaction was rejected. A common misconception is that endorsement or channel policies alone enforce application semantics; they do not. The takeaway is to treat chaincode as the last trust boundary where business rules and least privilege must be enforced.

Fabric exposes a ClientIdentity object from the transaction context that gives you verified facts about the submitter. The most commonly used methods are GetMSPID, which returns the submitter's organization's MSP ID; GetID, which returns a unique identifier derived from the certificate; GetX509Certificate, which returns the entire certificate for advanced parsing; and GetAttributeValue, which fetches custom attributes embedded in the X.509 certificate. Use GetMSPID for organization-level checks such as allowing only Org1MSP to create certain objects. Use GetAttributeValue when you need role-level control—an example is rejecting DeleteDocument unless the caller has role:admin. GetX509Certificate is powerful but more complex: parsing the certificate to inspect OU or CN fields is possible but error-prone and may tighten coupling to CA configurations. A practical pattern is to prefer GetAttributeValue when the CA already emits attributes, because it's simpler and less brittle than manual certificate parsing. Remember to handle errors from these calls: identity retrieval can fail and should produce clear authorization errors. Which method you choose depends on the level of granularity and your CA's attribute provisioning. ClientIdentity methods you can rely on means choose getmspid for org checks, getattributevalue for abac role checks, and reserve getx509certificate for advanced parsing when necessary.. In practical terms, getmspid, getid, getx509certificate, getattributevalue — what they provide and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a transfer function pattern that enforces ownership by checking the caller's MSP. The chaincode reads the asset from world state, unmarshals it, retrieves ctx. GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID(), and then compares that MSP to the asset's Owner field. If they don't match, the chaincode returns an authorization error. This pattern prevents a client from simply passing a different owner value to circumvent checks. A concrete code example is in Go: the TransferAsset function gets the asset bytes, unmarshals into an Asset struct that includes Owner, calls GetClientIdentity(). GetMSPID(), and if callingClientMSPID!= asset. Owner it rejects. After authorization passes, the owner is updated and PutState writes the new asset. Deciding between MSP-based checks and ABAC using certificate attributes depends on the authorization granularity you need. MSP checks answer the question: 'Is the caller from organization X?' They are simple and stable, ideal for organization-level constraints like 'only Org1MSP may create documents'. ABAC answers role- or user-specific questions like 'is the caller an auditor or an admin?' when those roles are embedded as attributes in certificates. Use GetAttributeValue to read attributes such as role:admin and enforce role-based operations like DeleteDocument. A benefit of ABAC is flexibility: roles can be issued by the CA and changed by certificate management without code changes. But ABAC requires CA configuration to include attributes and careful handling of absent attributes. Transient data is a mechanism to pass confidential values to chaincode that should not be persisted to the world state. The client includes a transient map in the proposal; endorsing peers and chaincode see the data but only a hash is recorded on the ledger. GetTransient(), consumes the proof to validate the request, and then discards the sensitive value.
